title: Evaluation of Korean-Language COVID-19–Related Medical Information on YouTube: Cross-Sectional Infodemiology Study
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of the 200 most-viewed Korean-language COVID-19 YouTube videos (105 analysed after exclusions). Every video was classified useful vs misleading against KCDC guidelines by two physician coders, and the share of videos containing misleading information is reported with its denominator (39/105, 37.14%). That is an explicit truth/falsity judgement against an external ground truth (national health-authority guidelines plus an enumerated list of false claims), so it is CONTENT, not QUALITY, even though the paper also carries DISCERN/JAMAS/GQS quality scales.

estimates.date: Videos uploaded January 1, 2020 to April 30, 2020; metrics collected as of May 1, 2020
estimates.measure_type: % of the most-viewed Korean-language COVID-19 YouTube videos that contained misleading information
estimates.denominator: 105 Korean-language COVID-19 YouTube videos (the 200 most-viewed videos retrieved for 5 Korean keywords, minus 95 excluded as non-Korean, duplicated, irrelevant or livestreamed); 126,633,036 cumulative views
estimates.definition: A video was counted in the numerator if it contained ANY scientifically unproven information, judged against KCDC guidelines as of May 1, 2020; Textbox 1 enumerates the misleading statements (COVID-19 is a hoax, was weaponized, conspiracy theories about its origin, a food or supplement as cure/prevention, microchips under the guise of a vaccine, etc.)
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misleading videos were defined as those with scientifically unproven information, and we considered a video misleading if it contained any misleading information at all because it still had the potential to disseminate misinformation."
estimates.source_quote: Of the 105 total videos, 37.14% (39/105) contained misleading information
estimates.page_loc: Abstract (Results); the same figure appears in Results "Misleading Versus Useful Video" p. 5, in Table 1, and in the Discussion ("Out of 105 videos, 39 (37.14%) were found to be misleading.")
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two author-physicians who provided COVID-19 patient care in Korea independently reviewed and scored every video; KCDC (Korea Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) guidelines as of May 1, 2020 were the standard for scientific correctness; discrepancies resolved by discussion; Cohen kappa for the usefulness classification (and for source classification) = 1, i.e. full agreement
estimates.moderator_quote: A total 200 of the most extensively viewed videos were screened from the YouTube video application programming interface. The search criteria used to obtain the videos comprised of the following terms in Korean: "Coronavirus," "COVID," "Corona," "Wuhan virus," and "Wuhan pneumonia." ... KCDC guidelines as of May 1, 2020, were used as a standard to determine whether a video's content was scientifically correct.
estimates.notes: Headline prevalence row for the paper. Denominator is rank-truncated (top-200 most viewed on a COVID-19 keyword search), hence denom_selection=curated; the 37.14% is a share of popular videos, not of all Korean COVID-19 videos on YouTube. Uploaders include YouTubers based outside Korea who made Korean-language videos, so the country label is language-defined rather than strictly geographic.

estimates.date: Videos uploaded January 1, 2020 to April 30, 2020; metrics collected as of May 1, 2020
estimates.measure_type: % of independent user-generated Korean-language COVID-19 YouTube videos that contained misleading information
estimates.denominator: 47 videos uploaded by independent users (individuals who are not health care professionals and have no established affiliation), a subset of the 105 analysed videos
estimates.definition: Same numerator rule as the overall row: the video contained any scientifically unproven information judged against KCDC guidelines
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misleading videos were defined as those with scientifically unproven information, and we considered a video misleading if it contained any misleading information at all because it still had the potential to disseminate misinformation."
estimates.source_quote: independent user–generated videos showed the highest proportion of misleading information at 68.09% (32/47), while all of the government-generated videos were useful.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract (Results); same figure in Results p. 5 and Table 1 (Source, n (%))
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two physician coders and same KCDC-guideline standard as the overall row; kappa = 1 for both the source classification and the usefulness classification
estimates.moderator_quote: Independent users are individuals who are not health care professionals and have no established affiliation, and we included YouTubers from both Korea and other countries who made Korean-language videos.
estimates.notes: ADJUDICATOR: this is a source-type SUBGROUP of the same 105 videos, kept only because it is one of the paper's two headline findings (it is stated in the Abstract). It must NOT be pooled alongside the 37.14% overall row - use one or the other. The complementary headline (government agency videos 0/8 misleading, 0%) is verbatim too but rests on n=8, so it was not given its own row; news agencies 4/39 (10.26%) and health care professionals 3/11 (27.27%) are in Table 1 and were left out for the same reason.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Not extracted, deliberately: the remaining source-type cells of Table 1 (news agencies 4/39, 10.26%; health care professionals 3/11, 27.27%; government agencies 0/8, 0.00%) - verbatim but small-n subgroups of the same corpus. (2) DISCERN, JAMAS, GQS, TCCI and MICI are reported only as medians with IQRs, never as a share of videos above a threshold, so per section 3 of the instructions they generate no row (and DISCERN/GQS/JAMAS would be construct QUALITY in any case). (3) "In this study, most of the misleading information was delivered by independent users (32/39, 82.05%)" is a share of the misleading videos attributable to one source class - it is a composition statistic, not a prevalence, and it is not a top-X%-of-sources -> Y%-of-activity pair, so no CONCENTRATION row was created (R1 would fail: no conc_group_pct/conc_share_pct pair is stated). (4) MICI content-coverage percentages (e.g. 74.24% covered "transmission and precautionary measures") are shares of videos covering a topic, not shares that are false - no row. (5) The DISCERN/GQS/TCCI comparisons in Table 2 are computed only among the 66 USEFUL videos, so they cannot yield a prevalence figure. (6) Figures quoted from other papers (English videos 19/69, 27.5%; Mandarin/English comparisons from Khatri et al and Li et al) are excluded per R8 as figures the paper cites from elsewhere.

rob.design: Cross-sectional infodemiology content analysis. Frame: YouTube Data API, 5 Korean-language keywords ("Coronavirus", "COVID", "Corona", "Wuhan virus", "Wuhan pneumonia"), 1,610,865 videos returned, the 200 most-viewed screened, 95 excluded (non-Korean, duplicated, irrelevant, livestreamed), 105 analysed (126,633,036 views), uploads 1 Jan - 30 Apr 2020, metrics as of 1 May 2020. Coding: two author-physicians reviewed and scored every video independently, discrepancies resolved by discussion; ground truth for correctness was KCDC guidelines as of 1 May 2020, with an enumerated list of misleading statements (Textbox 1). Reliability as reported: Cohen kappa = 1 for both source classification and usefulness classification; ICCs for the scaled instruments were DISCERN 0.47 (95% CI -0.29 to 0.81), JAMAS 0.93 (0.80-0.98), GQS 0.71 (0.17-0.90), TCCI 0.89 (0.70-0.96), MICI 0.91 (0.73-0.97). No viewer-level data collected. IRB-exempt (CR-20-102-L).
rob.item6_quote: Videos were classified as useful or misleading, and useful videos were defined as those with scientifically correct information. ... Misleading videos were defined as those with scientifically unproven information, and we considered a video misleading if it contained any misleading information at all because it still had the potential to disseminate misinformation.
rob.item10_quote: Of the total videos, 37.14% (39/105) contained misleading information. Independent user–generated videos showed the highest proportion of misleading information at 68.09% (32/47), while all the government-generated videos were useful.
